title: Joshua 3:1–6
context: Joshua 3 opens the long-awaited crossing into the land promised to the patriarchs. After the spies return from Jericho (chapter 2), Joshua leads Israel from Shittim to the Jordan, where they wait three days, recalling the timetable announced in 1:11. The officers instruct the people to follow the ark of the covenant, carried by the Levitical priests, while keeping a wide space between themselves and it. Joshua calls the people to sanctify themselves because the LORD will do wonders the next day, and the priests take up the ark and go ahead. The ark, the sign of God’s covenant presence, leads the way, and Israel follows. Both traditions read these verses as shared ground: God goes before his people, he deserves reverent preparation, and he leads them on a way they have not traveled before. The passage is narrative and procedural rather than a text about the order of salvation, so the notes do not force a doctrinal fork onto it.

verses.text: Joshua got up early in the morning; and they moved from Shittim and came to the Jordan, he and all the children of Israel. They camped there before they crossed over.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua rises early and moves the whole people from Shittim to the edge of the Jordan, where they camp before crossing. The leader acts promptly on the word he received in chapter 1, and the people move with him.

Arminian readers see here the readiness of faith: God has promised the land, and Joshua responds by acting on that promise without delay. Obedience is not the cause of the promise, but it is the fitting, willing response of people who trust the God who gave it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shittim was where Israel had sinned at Baal Peor (Numbers 25), so the move from there to the Jordan marks a turning from a place of failure toward the fulfillment of God’s promise.

Reformed readers stress that the initiative belongs to God, who promised the land to Abraham and now brings his people to the threshold. Joshua’s early rising is real obedience, and both traditions agree that it flows from trust in what God has already pledged to do.

verses.text: After three days, the officers went through the middle of the camp;
verses.arminianNotes:
The three days of waiting recall the instruction in 1:11, where the officers told the people to prepare food because they would cross within three days. The officers now move through the camp to give the next orders.

Arminian readers note that God works through ordered leadership and clear communication. The people are not swept along without understanding; they are told what to do and given time to prepare, so that their following is informed and responsive.
verses.reformedNotes:
The pause at the river is part of the narrative’s careful pacing, and the officers’ circuit through the camp shows that the whole nation is being organized for a single act of obedience.

Reformed readers see God governing even the timing and logistics of his people’s journey. Both traditions agree that ordinary administration, such as officers relaying instructions, is one of the means God uses to accomplish his purposes.

verses.text: and they commanded the people, saying, “When you see the ark of the LORD your God’s covenant, and the Levitical priests bearing it, then leave your place and follow it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are told that when they see “the ark of the LORD your God’s covenant” carried by the Levitical priests, they must leave their place and follow it. The ark, not Joshua or the army, sets the direction.

Arminian readers emphasize the call to follow: God goes first, and his people must respond by moving when he moves. Divine leading invites a real human answer, and the people’s willingness to leave their place is part of the story of faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ark represents God’s covenant presence and his throne among his people, so the command to follow it means that God himself leads Israel into the land.

Reformed readers stress that God goes before his people and that their path is set by his covenant, not by their own strategy. Both traditions agree that the order of the verse matters: God leads, and his people follow.

verses.text: Yet there shall be a space between you and it of about two thousand cubits by measure—don’t come closer to it—that you may know the way by which you must go; for you have not passed this way before.”
verses.arminianNotes:
A space of about two thousand cubits must separate the people from the ark, so that they may see the way they are to go, “for you have not passed this way before.” The distance serves both reverence and visibility.

Arminian readers note that the instruction protects reverence while keeping the guide in plain sight. God does not hide the way from his people; he makes it visible so that they can follow with understanding into territory none of them has traveled.
verses.reformedNotes:
The distance guards the holiness of the ark, which Israel had learned not to approach casually, and it allows the whole people to keep the ark in view as they move.

Reformed readers see a lesson in holy distance and gracious guidance held together: God is holy, yet he leads his people on a path they do not know. Both traditions agree that the verse joins reverence for God’s presence with trust in his direction.

verses.text: Joshua said to the people, “Sanctify yourselves; for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua calls the people to sanctify themselves because the LORD will do wonders among them the next day. Preparation for God’s act is a matter of holiness, not merely of packing supplies.

Arminian readers stress that God calls his people to prepare their hearts and lives to receive what he is about to do. Consecration is a real response that God asks of them, and it expresses expectant faith in the wonders he has promised.
verses.reformedNotes:
The call to consecration echoes Israel’s preparation at Sinai before God appeared (Exodus 19), and it sets the crossing in the frame of worship rather than military maneuver.

Reformed readers note that the wonders are entirely the LORD’s work, while the people’s sanctifying of themselves is the fitting posture of those about to witness it. Both traditions agree that God’s mighty acts call for holy preparation and reverent expectation.

verses.text: Joshua spoke to the priests, saying, “Take up the ark of the covenant, and cross over before the people.” They took up the ark of the covenant, and went before the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua tells the priests to take up the ark of the covenant and cross over before the people, and they do exactly as commanded. The verse moves from instruction to obedience without delay.

Arminian readers see here a model of responsive obedience: the priests do what they are told, trusting that God will act when they step forward. Their willingness to go first, carrying the sign of God’s presence, shows faith that acts on God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The priests carry the ark ahead of the people, so the symbol of God’s presence physically leads the nation toward the river.

Reformed readers stress that God’s presence goes before his people as the ground of their safety and success. Both traditions agree that the priests’ prompt obedience and the leading of the ark belong together, and that the scene prepares for God’s decisive act at the water.
